messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Mariana

Mariana was twenty-two when the bomb went off at the transit hub downtown. She had been standing in line at the coffee kiosk, waiting for her shift at the warehouse to start, when the blast came—a sound so complete it seemed to erase everything before it. The percussion threw her backward. Her ears rang with a frequency that felt like it was coming from inside her own skull. Around her, people screamed, but their voices sounded distant, muffled, as though she were underwater. She remembered the smell—acrid, chemical, mixed with something burnt and organic that she could not name. She remembered running, her legs moving without her consent, her body taking over while her mind seemed to fracture into separate pieces. There were gaps in what came after: she could not recall how she got out of the building, could not picture the faces of the people she must have passed, could not remember the exact moment she realized she was bleeding from a cut on her shoulder. When she tried to fill in those blanks later, in the safety of her apartment, the effort made her feel as though she were drowning all over again.

The months that followed were a slow erosion. What frightened Mariana most was that she had come to believe the world was fundamentally dangerous—that the randomness of that day was not an aberration but a glimpse of reality. If it could happen at a coffee kiosk on an ordinary Tuesday, it could happen anywhere. This conviction fed her need to be constantly on guard, scanning every room the moment she entered it, noting exits, watching the hands and bodies of people around her. At the warehouse, where she had worked for three years, her hypervigilance became a visible thing. She positioned herself near the loading dock, away from crowds of coworkers. She tracked the movements of the forklift operators obsessively, her body tensing whenever someone moved too quickly or unexpectedly. Her supervisor had begun to notice. She was making mistakes—missing inventory counts because she was too busy watching the perimeter—and her coworkers had started giving her a wide berth, unsettled by the intensity of her gaze, the way she flinched if someone approached from her blind side.

The gaps in her memory of the event felt like proof that her own body had betrayed her. She knew, in a factual way, that she had survived, that she had made it out, but she could not locate herself within the narrative of those missing minutes. This absence terrified her because it suggested her body might fail her again without warning. She no longer trusted it to protect her or to respond correctly in a crisis. When she tried to talk to her sister about what had happened, the words simply would not come. She knew the sequence of events—the sound, the fall, the running—but when she opened her mouth to describe it, something seized in her throat. The only feeling that came through clearly was rage, a burning fury at the randomness, at her own helplessness, at the fact that she had survived when others had not. That rage would surge without warning, often triggered by small things: a car backfiring, a door slamming, a sudden movement in her peripheral vision. In those moments, she felt as though she might explode, and the intensity of the anger terrified her almost as much as the fear itself.

To manage the constant threat she perceived, Mariana began to deliberately disconnect from her body and her surroundings. She would sit in the break room at work and practice a kind of deliberate blankness, letting her mind drift to a place where the warehouse, the noise, the watching eyes of her coworkers did not exist. She avoided eye contact religiously—looking directly at someone felt like a vulnerability, an exposure. If she did not meet their gaze, she reasoned, she could not see the moment their intentions shifted, but more importantly, they could not see into her. These strategies offered temporary relief, a brief reprieve from the exhausting vigilance. Yet each time she dissociated, each time she looked away, she felt her world shrink a little more. The avoidance itself became evidence that danger was real, that her fear was justified. The more she withdrew, the more isolated she became, and the more isolated she became, the more the world seemed hostile and unknowable. By the time she turned twenty-four, she had stopped going to her cousin's gatherings, had turned down a promotion that would have required her to train new staff, and had begun to dread the walk from her car to the warehouse entrance each morning.

Two months ago, a coworker's sudden movement—he had reached past her without warning—sent Mariana into a panic so acute that she left work and did not return for a week. When she finally came back, she knew something had to change. She was failing at the one thing she had managed to hold onto: her job. The thought of losing it terrified her more than anything else, because it would mean admitting that the bomb had taken everything. She called a therapist, hands shaking as she dialed, and when asked what she most wanted to work on, she said, simply, "I need to stop being afraid of everything." What she did not say, but what hung unspoken in the room, was that she did not know if she still knew how.

violation_explanations: Negative appraisals (distorted beliefs about danger and self-blame) are described extensively, and maladaptive strategies (dissociation, avoidance, disconnection) are clearly present, but no paragraph conveys that her negative beliefs directly drive her coping strategies—the causal link is missing.

Threat perception is described throughout, and intrusive memories of the trauma appear, but no paragraph establishes that the sense of threat leads to or triggers the traumatic memory itself—this directional causal relationship is absent.
